title: 51. LocalStorage & SessionStorage
theory:
Both allow saving key/value pairs in the browser.
LocalStorage: Survives browser restarts. No expiration.
SessionStorage: Cleared when the page session ends (tab closed).
Data is saved as strings only. Use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.

title: 52. Object-Oriented JS (OOP)
theory: OOP in JS is prototype-based. An object acts as a template for other objects to inherit properties and methods. Before ES6, constructor functions were used to implement OOP.

title: 53. Prototypes & Prototypal Inheritance
theory: Every JS object has a hidden property [[Prototype]] (accessed via __proto__). When you access a property, JS looks at the object, then its prototype, then prototype's prototype (Prototype Chain) until it finds it or reaches null.

title: 54. ES6 Classes
theory: ES6 introduced 'class' syntax. It is mostly syntactic sugar over Constructor Functions and Prototypes, but makes OOP look cleaner, similar to Java or C++.

title: 55. Class Inheritance
theory: Use the 'extends' keyword to inherit from another class. The 'super()' method must be called inside the constructor to execute the parent constructor.

title: 56. Call, Apply, Bind
theory:
Methods to manually set the value of 'this' when calling a function.
call(obj, arg1, arg2)
apply(obj, [argsArray])
bind(obj, arg1) -> Returns a NEW function, does not execute immediately.

title: 57. Default Parameters
theory: Introduced in ES6, default parameters allow named parameters to be initialized with default values if no value or 'undefined' is passed.

title: 58. Template Literals
output: > My name is John. I am 20.
theory: Enclosed by backticks (`), template literals allow multi-line strings and string interpolation (embedding variables inside strings) using ${variable}. No more messy string concatenation!

title: 59. Modules (Import / Export)
theory:
Modules allow you to split your JS into multiple files. You 'export' variables/functions from one file and 'import' them into another.
Note: Requires <script type="module"> in HTML.

title: 60. Optional Chaining (?.)
theory: Provides a safe way to access deeply nested object properties without throwing a "Cannot read property of undefined" error if an intermediate property is null/undefined.

title: 61. Nullish Coalescing (??)
theory: Returns its right-hand side operand when its left-hand side operand is null or undefined. Better than the || operator because || triggers on falsy values like 0 or "", whereas ?? only triggers on null/undefined.

title: 62. Set and Map
theory:
Set: A collection of UNIQUE values. Adding a duplicate has no effect.
Map: A collection of Key-Value pairs where keys can be ANY type (objects, functions), unlike normal Objects where keys must be strings.

title: 63. Shallow vs Deep Copy
theory: Shallow Copy (using Spread or Object.assign) only copies the first level. Nested objects are still referenced! Deep Copy clones everything recursively.

title: 64. Generators (function*)
theory: Generators are functions that can be paused and exited, and later re-entered. Their context (variable bindings) is saved across re-entrances. You use 'yield' to pause.

title: 65. Strict Mode
theory: Adding 'use strict'; at the top of a file or function enables strict mode. It catches common coding bloopers, throwing exceptions (e.g., using undeclared variables).

title: 66. Web Storage vs Cookies
theory:
LocalStorage: 5MB limit, no expiration, never sent to server.
Cookies: 4KB limit, expires, sent with EVERY HTTP request.
SessionStorage: Cleared when tab closes.

title: 67. Garbage Collection
theory: JS uses 'Mark and Sweep' garbage collection. It periodically checks the memory for objects that are no longer 'reachable' from the global root. If an object is unreachable, its memory is freed.

title: 68. Typeof and Instanceof
theory: 'typeof' is used for primitives. However, typeof null is 'object' (a famous JS bug). 'instanceof' is used to check if an object is an instance of a specific class or constructor.
code:
console.log(typeof 'hi'); // 'string'
console.log(typeof null); // 'object'

const arr = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(typeof arr); // 'object'

// Better check for arrays
console.log(arr instanceof Array); // true
console.log(Array.isArray(arr)); // true

title: 69. Date Object
theory: The Date object is used for working with dates and times. Under the hood, it stores dates as the number of milliseconds since Jan 1, 1970 (Unix Epoch).

title: 70. Math Object
theory: Math is a built-in object that has properties and methods for mathematical constants and functions. It's not a constructor.

title: 71. Symbols (ES6)
theory: Symbols are unique and immutable primitives. They are often used to add unique property keys to an object that won't collide with keys any other code might add to the object.

title: 72. Iterables & Iterators
theory: An iterable is a data structure that wants to make its elements accessible to the public (Arrays, Strings, Maps, Sets). It implements the Symbol.iterator method.

title: 73. Fetching APIs (Advanced)
theory: Fetch isn't just for GET requests. You can pass an options object to make POST, PUT, or DELETE requests and send JSON payloads in the body.

title: 74. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
theory: A security mechanism built into browsers. If your frontend on 'domain-a.com' tries to fetch data from 'api.com', the browser blocks it unless 'api.com' explicitly sends CORS headers allowing 'domain-a.com'.

title: 75. End of Masterclass
theory:
Congratulations! You have covered JavaScript from basic syntax to the depths of the Event Loop and advanced OOP.
Remember: Reading is only 20%. The other 80% is writing code. Go build projects!
